newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada's Prairie crop output seen at or above par.
newsitem.headline: Canada's Prairie crop output seen at or above par.

text.p: Canada's Prairie crop output on Thursday was forecast to be above average in the west and about average in the east, crop specialists said.

"I'd say it's an above average rating of crop condition at this time and it's probably ahead of normal in terms of crop development, so things bode well from a crop production side," said Mike Makowsky, a Saskatchewan Agriculture grain analyst.
Statistics Canada's June 27 forecast set western Canadian wheat acreage at 21.955 million acres and 28.236 million acres for all of Canada.

The latest production estimate issued by the International Grains Institute on Thursday, however, cut Canada's output outlook to 25.5 million tonnes from 27 million due to "a major shift to canola, flaxseed and other more profitable crops."

While western Canadian wheat area was down 10 percent compared to the prior year and canola acreage was projected to rise 38 percent by StatsCan, wheat yield prospects were expected to fare better than canola, experts said.
The northwest Prairies saw more rain than usual since April while the southeast was drier than normal. Wheat sustains hot, dry weather better than oilseeds.

"Northern Alberta's been very moist and in some cases they've stopped seeding but there's still that dry horseshoe shaped area from southeast Saskatchewan to southern Alberta," said Rick Raddatz, Environment Canada soil scientist.
"The rains of the last week bumped up soil moisture in Manitoba," Raddatz added.
All types of wheat were expected to yield more bushels per acre in Alberta than the five year average.
"We've got good growth," said Wendy Boje, Alberta Agriculture crop analyst. "Statistics Canada...showed Alberta crops were doing better than Saskatchewan or Manitoba."
Crop specialists in Saskatchewan and Manitoba declined to give specific yield forecasts.
"Half the province's production should be above average," Saskatchewan Ag's Makowsky said.
Another 10 to 15 percent were rated poor to very poor due to drought conditions in the southeast and south central districts and the balance should yield average crops, he said.
"If conditions remain the same, we'll get close to an average crop," Manitoba Agriculture analyst Al Sturko said.
